{{draft}} [[Category:Completion tier 7]] {{Infobox deity|image=Three-storied_Pagoda_of_Seiganto-ji_and_Nachi_Falls_201808.jpg|caption=Three-storied [[Pagoda|Pagoda]] of {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Nachi Falls|en}}|name=Kumano Gongen|cult_centre={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|cult_center={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}}} {{complex}} {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano (deity)|lt=Kumano|ja|熊野権現|en|Draft:Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen}}|熊野権現}}, also known as {{nihongo|Three Mountains of Kumano|熊野三山}}Encyclopedia of Shinto, [http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1076 Kumano Shinkō], accessed on October 6, 2008[http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm Kumano Sanzan] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609225919/http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm|date=2008-06-09}}, World Heritage Registration Association, accessed on October 13, 2008, is a Japanese deity associated with [[Kumano shrine|Kumano Shrines]].{{Cite web|date=2022-07-04|title=Discover the unique spiritual culture of Kumano with exclusive insight from a chief priest at Kumano Hongu Taisha|url=https://www.the-kansai-guide.com/en/article/item/20036/|access-date=2024-03-11|website=The KANSAI Guide - The Origin of Japan, KANSAI|language=en}} The kami enshrined in the three Kumano Sanzan Grand Shrines and worshipped in [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrines]] are the three Kumano mountains: Hongū, Shingū, and Nachi. There are more than 3,000 Kumano shrines in [[Japan|Japan]], and each has received its [[kami|kami]] from another Kumano shrine through a process of propagation called {{ill|''{{ill|bunrei|en}}''|分霊|1=Bunrei}} or {{ill|''{{ill|kanjō|en}}''|勧請|lt=Enshrinement|1=Kanjō|2=ja|3=分霊|4=es|5=Bunrei|6=id|7=Kanjō|8=zh|9=分靈|10=fr|11=Kanjō|lt=Kanjō}}. The point of origin of the Kumano cult is the Kumano Sanzan shrine complex in {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en}}, which comprises {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en}}|熊野速玉大社}} ({{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en}}), {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en}} ({{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en}}) and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en}} ({{ill|Nachikatsuura|en}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en}}).{{Cite web|title=Sacred site "Kumano Sanzan"|url=http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|archive-date=2009-03-03|access-date=2008-06-12}} == Origins == [[Image:Kumano Jinja 12.jpg|275 px|thumb|A [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrine]]]]The three Kumano Sanzan shrines are the ''Sōhonsha'' ("head shrines") of all Kumano shrines and lie between 20 and 40 km from each other. They are connected to each other by the pilgrimage route known as {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|熊野古道}}. The great Kumano Sanzan complex also includes two Buddhist temples, {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Fudarakusan-ji|en}}.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Sanzan|url=http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822161901/http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|archive-date=2019-08-22|access-date=2014-10-15}} {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi}}, the fifth and youngest child of [[Amaterasu]] is sometimes linked to Kumano Gongen The deity's name, Kusubi (Kusuhi), is thought to mean "strange spirit" (mysterious divine spirit) or "strange fire. The current deity of [[Kumano Taisha|Kumano-taisha]] is "{{Nihongo|2=熊野大神櫛御気野命|3=Kumano Oyagami Kushimitama no Mikoto}}," but there is a theory that the original deity was Kumanokusubi. There is a theory that the deity of {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en}}, {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi}}, is [[Izanami|Izamiami]], but this is also believed to be a reference to Kumanokusubi.{{Cite book|title="Nihon no kami yomi kakkai jiten"|publisher=Kashiwa Shobo|others=Kawaguchi Kenji (ed.)|year=1999|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3|language=ja}} The religious significance of the Kumano region goes back to prehistoric times and therefore predates all modern religions in Japan. The area is still considered a place of physical healing. Each shrine initially had its own separate form of nature worship. In the 10th century, under the influence of Buddhism, the three came to be worshiped together as the three deities of Kumano. Because at the time Japanese ''kami'' were believed to be emanations of {{ill|Buddha|lt=buddhas|en}} (''{{ill|honji suijaku|en}}'' theory), the three came to be associated with Buddhas. Kuniyasutamahime became associated with ''Sahasrabhūja'' {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en}} (''Senju Kannon'', "{{ill|Avalokiteśvara#Thousand-armed Avalokiteśvara|lt=Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara|en}}"), {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}} (''Yakushi Nyōrai'') and {{ill|Amitābha|en}} (''Amida Nyōrai'').{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sZmMAQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|last1=Breen|first1=John|last2=Teeuwen|first2=Mark|publisher=Taylor & Francis|year=2013|isbn=978-1-136-82704-4|page=194|authorlink1=John Breen (scholar)|authorlink2=Mark Teeuwen}} Kumano Gongen refers to the deities of the Three Kumano Mountains, especially focusing on the main deities: Ketsumiko ({{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊}}), Hayatama ({{ill|Izanagi|lt=Izanagi|ja|イザナギ}}), and Musubi (also written as Fusubi or Musubi, or "Yui" for {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ}}), collectively known as the Kumano Sanjo Gongen. In addition to these, other deities are also included, referred to as the Kumano Jūniso Gongen. The site became a unique example of {{ill|shinbutsu-shūgō|en}}, the fusion between Buddhism and Japanese {{ill|ethnic religion|lt=indigenous religion|en}}. The Three Kumano Mountains consist of Kumano Hongū Taisha, Kumano Hayatama Taisha, and Kumano Nachi Taisha.{{Cite web|date=2009-03-03|title=Sacred Site, "Kumano Sanzan"|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=web.archive.org}} Initially, they developed separately; Hongū was established during the reign of [[Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suinin]], Hayatama during [[Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō's]] reign (according to the Fusang Jijin), and Nachi during [[Emperor Kōshō|Emperor Kōshō's]] reign, with the foundation involving a practice called naked pilgrimage (also "naked form") , though this is uncertain. In official histories, the names of the deities can be confirmed in documents from 806, with a record from 766 mentioning that four households were dedicated to the Hayatama and Kumano Musubi deities, indicating that these two deities were worshipped together in what is today Shingu, known as Kumano Shinson.[[Image:Waterfall Nachi02.jpg|thumb|200 px|{{ill|Nachi Falls|en}}]] By the mid-9th century, the deity was simply called Kumano Imasu Kami, and the main deity of Hongū, previously unclear, began to be called Ketsumiko or Shōshō Bosatsu, along with New Musubi and Hayatama, establishing the tradition that Ketsumiko was an ancient Kumano deity ("Kumano Gongen Suijaku Engi", included in "Chōkan Kanmon" ). The Kumano Sanzan site attracted many worshipers and became a popular pilgrimage destination. In the 11th century, pilgrims were mostly members of the {{ill|emperor of Japan|lt=imperial family|en}} or aristocrats, but four centuries later they were mostly commoners. The visit was referred to as the {{nihongo|"Kumano ant pilgrimage"|蟻の熊野参り||Ari no Kumano mairi}}, because they could be seen winding through the valleys like so many ants. Moreover, the "Chūyūki" entry for October 26, 1109, not only lists these three deities but also mentions Goshodenji, Ichiman Kenzoku, Jūman Kongō Dōji, Kanjō Jūgoso, Hikō Yasha, and Meiji Kongō Dōji, and the pilgrimage records of Toba-in and Taikenmon'in (included in "Chōshūki") from February 1, Longsheng 3 year, list the twelve Gongen and their original Buddhas, showing that by this time, the Kumano Sanjo Gongen and Jūniso Gongen were established . Nachi, differing in nature from Hongū and Hayatama and known as a sacred place for waterfall asceticism, initially had {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ}} as the main deity, but by the early Kamakura period, the "Kumano Gongen Kongō Zōjō Hōden Constructing Merits Diary" included tales related to the worship of the Twelve Gongen, indicating that by this time, the deities of Hongū and Hayatama were also enshrined there. Thus, by the end of the 12th century, the three mountains had unified by worshipping each other's deities . == Kumano Gongen == Each of the Three Mountains is considered to represent a different pure land: Hongū represents the [[Sukhavati|Western Paradise]], Shingu represents the eastern pure land of Lapis Lazuli{{Efn|the eastern pure land of Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa "Pure Lapis Lazuli" ruled by {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}}}}, and Nachi represents the Southern Potalaka{{efn|Ratnasambhava, the Buddha of the Southern Pure Land}}. From the [[Heian period]] onward, Kumano as a whole came to be regarded as a land of the Pure Land. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|1=Bhaisajyaguru|lt=Yakushi Nyorai (Me)dicine Buddha|en}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en:draft|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|12=fr}} {{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}} The {{ill|Nachi Falls|en}} is said to be the thirteenth member.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|url=https://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/en/kumano-sanzan/nachi.html|access-date=2024-03-24|website=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|language=en}} At {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en}} and {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en}}, twelve deities are enshrined as follows. {| class="wikitable" |+'''Kumano Twelve Shrines GongenMiyaie [1992: 60] according to the table''' ! {{draft}} {{Infobox deity|image=Three-storied_Pagoda_of_Seiganto-ji_and_Nachi_Falls_201808.jpg|caption=Three-storied [[Pagoda|Pagoda]] of {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Nachi Falls|en|12=draft}}|name=Kumano Gongen|cult_centre={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|cult_center={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|12=draft}}}} {{complex}} {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano (deity)|lt=Kumano|ja|熊野権現|en|Draft:Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|12=draft}}|熊野権現}}, also known as {{nihongo|Three Mountains of Kumano|熊野三山}}Encyclopedia of Shinto, [http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1076 Kumano Shinkō], accessed on October 6, 2008[http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm Kumano Sanzan] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609225919/http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm|date=2008-06-09}}, World Heritage Registration Association, accessed on October 13, 2008, is a Japanese deity associated with [[Kumano shrine|Kumano Shrines]].{{Cite web|date=2022-07-04|title=Discover the unique spiritual culture of Kumano with exclusive insight from a chief priest at Kumano Hongu Taisha|url=https://www.the-kansai-guide.com/en/article/item/20036/|access-date=2024-03-11|website=The KANSAI Guide - The Origin of Japan, KANSAI|language=en}} The kami enshrined in the three Kumano Sanzan Grand Shrines and worshipped in [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrines]] are the three Kumano mountains: Hongū, Shingū, and Nachi. There are more than 3,000 Kumano shrines in [[Japan|Japan]], and each has received its [[kami|kami]] from another Kumano shrine through a process of propagation called {{ill|''{{ill|bunrei|en}}''|分霊|1=Bunrei}} or {{ill|''{{ill|kanjō|en}}''|勧請|lt=Enshrinement|1=Kanjō|2=ja|3=分霊|4=es|5=Bunrei|6=id|7=Kanjō|8=zh|9=分靈|10=fr|11=Kanjō|lt=Kanjō}}. The point of origin of the Kumano cult is the Kumano Sanzan shrine complex in {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en}}, which comprises {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en|12=draft}}|熊野速玉大社}} ({{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en}}), {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en|12=draft}} ({{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en}}) and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en|12=draft}} ({{ill|Nachikatsuura|en}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|12=draft}}).{{Cite web|title=Sacred site "Kumano Sanzan"|url=http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|archive-date=2009-03-03|access-date=2008-06-12}} == Origins == [[Image:Kumano Jinja 12.jpg|275 px|thumb|A [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrine]]]]The three Kumano Sanzan shrines are the ''Sōhonsha'' ("head shrines") of all Kumano shrines and lie between 20 and 40 km from each other. They are connected to each other by the pilgrimage route known as {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|熊野古道|12=draft}}. The great Kumano Sanzan complex also includes two Buddhist temples, {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Fudarakusan-ji|en|12=draft}}.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Sanzan|url=http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822161901/http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|archive-date=2019-08-22|access-date=2014-10-15}} {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|12=draft}}, the fifth and youngest child of [[Amaterasu]] is sometimes linked to Kumano Gongen The deity's name, Kusubi (Kusuhi), is thought to mean "strange spirit" (mysterious divine spirit) or "strange fire. The current deity of [[Kumano Taisha|Kumano-taisha]] is "{{Nihongo|2=熊野大神櫛御気野命|3=Kumano Oyagami Kushimitama no Mikoto}}," but there is a theory that the original deity was Kumanokusubi. There is a theory that the deity of {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en}}, {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|12=draft}}, is [[Izanami|Izamiami]], but this is also believed to be a reference to Kumanokusubi.{{Cite book|title="Nihon no kami yomi kakkai jiten"|publisher=Kashiwa Shobo|others=Kawaguchi Kenji (ed.)|year=1999|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3|language=ja}} The religious significance of the Kumano region goes back to prehistoric times and therefore predates all modern religions in Japan. The area is still considered a place of physical healing. Each shrine initially had its own separate form of nature worship. In the 10th century, under the influence of Buddhism, the three came to be worshiped together as the three deities of Kumano. Because at the time Japanese ''kami'' were believed to be emanations of {{ill|Buddha|lt=buddhas|en|12=draft}} (''{{ill|honji suijaku|en}}'' theory), the three came to be associated with Buddhas. Kuniyasutamahime became associated with ''Sahasrabhūja'' {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|12=draft}} (''Senju Kannon'', "{{ill|Avalokiteśvara#Thousand-armed Avalokiteśvara|lt=Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara|en}}"), {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}} (''Yakushi Nyōrai'') and {{ill|Amitābha|en|12=draft}} (''Amida Nyōrai'').{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sZmMAQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|last1=Breen|first1=John|last2=Teeuwen|first2=Mark|publisher=Taylor & Francis|year=2013|isbn=978-1-136-82704-4|page=194|authorlink1=John Breen (scholar)|authorlink2=Mark Teeuwen}} Kumano Gongen refers to the deities of the Three Kumano Mountains, especially focusing on the main deities: Ketsumiko ({{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊|12=draft}}), Hayatama ({{ill|Izanagi|lt=Izanagi|ja|イザナギ|12=draft}}), and Musubi (also written as Fusubi or Musubi, or "Yui" for {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|12=draft}}), collectively known as the Kumano Sanjo Gongen. In addition to these, other deities are also included, referred to as the Kumano Jūniso Gongen. The site became a unique example of {{ill|shinbutsu-shūgō|en}}, the fusion between Buddhism and Japanese {{ill|ethnic religion|lt=indigenous religion|en|12=draft}}. The Three Kumano Mountains consist of Kumano Hongū Taisha, Kumano Hayatama Taisha, and Kumano Nachi Taisha.{{Cite web|date=2009-03-03|title=Sacred Site, "Kumano Sanzan"|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=web.archive.org}} Initially, they developed separately; Hongū was established during the reign of [[Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suinin]], Hayatama during [[Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō's]] reign (according to the Fusang Jijin), and Nachi during [[Emperor Kōshō|Emperor Kōshō's]] reign, with the foundation involving a practice called naked pilgrimage (also "naked form") , though this is uncertain. In official histories, the names of the deities can be confirmed in documents from 806, with a record from 766 mentioning that four households were dedicated to the Hayatama and Kumano Musubi deities, indicating that these two deities were worshipped together in what is today Shingu, known as Kumano Shinson.[[Image:Waterfall Nachi02.jpg|thumb|200 px|{{ill|Nachi Falls|en}}]] By the mid-9th century, the deity was simply called Kumano Imasu Kami, and the main deity of Hongū, previously unclear, began to be called Ketsumiko or Shōshō Bosatsu, along with New Musubi and Hayatama, establishing the tradition that Ketsumiko was an ancient Kumano deity ("Kumano Gongen Suijaku Engi", included in "Chōkan Kanmon" ). The Kumano Sanzan site attracted many worshipers and became a popular pilgrimage destination. In the 11th century, pilgrims were mostly members of the {{ill|emperor of Japan|lt=imperial family|en|12=draft}} or aristocrats, but four centuries later they were mostly commoners. The visit was referred to as the {{nihongo|"Kumano ant pilgrimage"|蟻の熊野参り||Ari no Kumano mairi}}, because they could be seen winding through the valleys like so many ants. Moreover, the "Chūyūki" entry for October 26, 1109, not only lists these three deities but also mentions Goshodenji, Ichiman Kenzoku, Jūman Kongō Dōji, Kanjō Jūgoso, Hikō Yasha, and Meiji Kongō Dōji, and the pilgrimage records of Toba-in and Taikenmon'in (included in "Chōshūki") from February 1, Longsheng 3 year, list the twelve Gongen and their original Buddhas, showing that by this time, the Kumano Sanjo Gongen and Jūniso Gongen were established . Nachi, differing in nature from Hongū and Hayatama and known as a sacred place for waterfall asceticism, initially had {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|12=draft}} as the main deity, but by the early Kamakura period, the "Kumano Gongen Kongō Zōjō Hōden Constructing Merits Diary" included tales related to the worship of the Twelve Gongen, indicating that by this time, the deities of Hongū and Hayatama were also enshrined there. Thus, by the end of the 12th century, the three mountains had unified by worshipping each other's deities . == Kumano Gongen == Each of the Three Mountains is considered to represent a different pure land: Hongū represents the [[Sukhavati|Western Paradise]], Shingu represents the eastern pure land of Lapis Lazuli{{Efn|the eastern pure land of Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa "Pure Lapis Lazuli" ruled by {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}}}}, and Nachi represents the Southern Potalaka{{efn|Ratnasambhava, the Buddha of the Southern Pure Land|12=draft}}. From the [[Heian period]] onward, Kumano as a whole came to be regarded as a land of the Pure Land. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en|12=draft}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|1=Bhaisajyaguru|lt=Yakushi Nyorai (Me)dicine Buddha|en|12=draft}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en:draft|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|12=fr|12=draft}} {{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}} The {{ill|Nachi Falls|en}} is said to be the thirteenth member.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|url=https://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/en/kumano-sanzan/nachi.html|access-date=2024-03-24|website=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|language=en|12=draft}} At {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en}} and {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en|12=draft}}, twelve deities are enshrined as follows. {| class="wikitable" |+'''Kumano Twelve Shrines GongenMiyaie [1992: 60] according to the table''' ! {{draft}} {{Infobox deity|image=Three-storied_Pagoda_of_Seiganto-ji_and_Nachi_Falls_201808.jpg|caption=Three-storied [[Pagoda|Pagoda]] of {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Nachi Falls|en|12=draft}}|name=Kumano Gongen|cult_centre={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|cult_center={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|12=draft}}}} {{complex}} {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano (deity)|lt=Kumano|ja|熊野権現|en|Draft:Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|12=draft}}|熊野権現}}, also known as {{nihongo|Three Mountains of Kumano|熊野三山}}Encyclopedia of Shinto, [http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1076 Kumano Shinkō], accessed on October 6, 2008[http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm Kumano Sanzan] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609225919/http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm|date=2008-06-09}}, World Heritage Registration Association, accessed on October 13, 2008, is a Japanese deity associated with [[Kumano shrine|Kumano Shrines]].{{Cite web|date=2022-07-04|title=Discover the unique spiritual culture of Kumano with exclusive insight from a chief priest at Kumano Hongu Taisha|url=https://www.the-kansai-guide.com/en/article/item/20036/|access-date=2024-03-11|website=The KANSAI Guide - The Origin of Japan, KANSAI|language=en}} The kami enshrined in the three Kumano Sanzan Grand Shrines and worshipped in [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrines]] are the three Kumano mountains: Hongū, Shingū, and Nachi. There are more than 3,000 Kumano shrines in [[Japan|Japan]], and each has received its [[kami|kami]] from another Kumano shrine through a process of propagation called {{ill|''{{ill|bunrei|en}}''|分霊|1=Bunrei}} or {{ill|''{{ill|kanjō|en}}''|勧請|lt=Enshrinement|1=Kanjō|2=ja|3=分霊|4=es|5=Bunrei|6=id|7=Kanjō|8=zh|9=分靈|10=fr|11=Kanjō|lt=Kanjō}}. The point of origin of the Kumano cult is the Kumano Sanzan shrine complex in {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en}}, which comprises {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en|12=draft}}|熊野速玉大社}} ({{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en}}), {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en|12=draft}} ({{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en}}) and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en|12=draft}} ({{ill|Nachikatsuura|en}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|12=draft}}).{{Cite web|title=Sacred site "Kumano Sanzan"|url=http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|archive-date=2009-03-03|access-date=2008-06-12}} == Origins == [[Image:Kumano Jinja 12.jpg|275 px|thumb|A [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrine]]]]The three Kumano Sanzan shrines are the ''Sōhonsha'' ("head shrines") of all Kumano shrines and lie between 20 and 40 km from each other. They are connected to each other by the pilgrimage route known as {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|熊野古道|12=draft}}. The great Kumano Sanzan complex also includes two Buddhist temples, {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Fudarakusan-ji|en|12=draft}}.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Sanzan|url=http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822161901/http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|archive-date=2019-08-22|access-date=2014-10-15}} {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|12=draft}}, the fifth and youngest child of [[Amaterasu]] is sometimes linked to Kumano Gongen The deity's name, Kusubi (Kusuhi), is thought to mean "strange spirit" (mysterious divine spirit) or "strange fire. The current deity of [[Kumano Taisha|Kumano-taisha]] is "{{Nihongo|2=熊野大神櫛御気野命|3=Kumano Oyagami Kushimitama no Mikoto}}," but there is a theory that the original deity was Kumanokusubi. There is a theory that the deity of {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en}}, {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|12=draft}}, is [[Izanami|Izamiami]], but this is also believed to be a reference to Kumanokusubi.{{Cite book|title="Nihon no kami yomi kakkai jiten"|publisher=Kashiwa Shobo|others=Kawaguchi Kenji (ed.)|year=1999|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3|language=ja}} The religious significance of the Kumano region goes back to prehistoric times and therefore predates all modern religions in Japan. The area is still considered a place of physical healing. Each shrine initially had its own separate form of nature worship. In the 10th century, under the influence of Buddhism, the three came to be worshiped together as the three deities of Kumano. Because at the time Japanese ''kami'' were believed to be emanations of {{ill|Buddha|lt=buddhas|en|12=draft}} (''{{ill|honji suijaku|en}}'' theory), the three came to be associated with Buddhas. Kuniyasutamahime became associated with ''Sahasrabhūja'' {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|12=draft}} (''Senju Kannon'', "{{ill|Avalokiteśvara#Thousand-armed Avalokiteśvara|lt=Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara|en}}"), {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}} (''Yakushi Nyōrai'') and {{ill|Amitābha|en|12=draft}} (''Amida Nyōrai'').{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sZmMAQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|last1=Breen|first1=John|last2=Teeuwen|first2=Mark|publisher=Taylor & Francis|year=2013|isbn=978-1-136-82704-4|page=194|authorlink1=John Breen (scholar)|authorlink2=Mark Teeuwen}} Kumano Gongen refers to the deities of the Three Kumano Mountains, especially focusing on the main deities: Ketsumiko ({{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊|12=draft}}), Hayatama ({{ill|Izanagi|lt=Izanagi|ja|イザナギ|12=draft}}), and Musubi (also written as Fusubi or Musubi, or "Yui" for {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|12=draft}}), collectively known as the Kumano Sanjo Gongen. In addition to these, other deities are also included, referred to as the Kumano Jūniso Gongen. The site became a unique example of {{ill|shinbutsu-shūgō|en}}, the fusion between Buddhism and Japanese {{ill|ethnic religion|lt=indigenous religion|en|12=draft}}. The Three Kumano Mountains consist of Kumano Hongū Taisha, Kumano Hayatama Taisha, and Kumano Nachi Taisha.{{Cite web|date=2009-03-03|title=Sacred Site, "Kumano Sanzan"|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=web.archive.org}} Initially, they developed separately; Hongū was established during the reign of [[Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suinin]], Hayatama during [[Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō's]] reign (according to the Fusang Jijin), and Nachi during [[Emperor Kōshō|Emperor Kōshō's]] reign, with the foundation involving a practice called naked pilgrimage (also "naked form") , though this is uncertain. In official histories, the names of the deities can be confirmed in documents from 806, with a record from 766 mentioning that four households were dedicated to the Hayatama and Kumano Musubi deities, indicating that these two deities were worshipped together in what is today Shingu, known as Kumano Shinson.[[Image:Waterfall Nachi02.jpg|thumb|200 px|{{ill|Nachi Falls|en}}]] By the mid-9th century, the deity was simply called Kumano Imasu Kami, and the main deity of Hongū, previously unclear, began to be called Ketsumiko or Shōshō Bosatsu, along with New Musubi and Hayatama, establishing the tradition that Ketsumiko was an ancient Kumano deity ("Kumano Gongen Suijaku Engi", included in "Chōkan Kanmon" ). The Kumano Sanzan site attracted many worshipers and became a popular pilgrimage destination. In the 11th century, pilgrims were mostly members of the {{ill|emperor of Japan|lt=imperial family|en|12=draft}} or aristocrats, but four centuries later they were mostly commoners. The visit was referred to as the {{nihongo|"Kumano ant pilgrimage"|蟻の熊野参り||Ari no Kumano mairi}}, because they could be seen winding through the valleys like so many ants. Moreover, the "Chūyūki" entry for October 26, 1109, not only lists these three deities but also mentions Goshodenji, Ichiman Kenzoku, Jūman Kongō Dōji, Kanjō Jūgoso, Hikō Yasha, and Meiji Kongō Dōji, and the pilgrimage records of Toba-in and Taikenmon'in (included in "Chōshūki") from February 1, Longsheng 3 year, list the twelve Gongen and their original Buddhas, showing that by this time, the Kumano Sanjo Gongen and Jūniso Gongen were established . Nachi, differing in nature from Hongū and Hayatama and known as a sacred place for waterfall asceticism, initially had {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|12=draft}} as the main deity, but by the early Kamakura period, the "Kumano Gongen Kongō Zōjō Hōden Constructing Merits Diary" included tales related to the worship of the Twelve Gongen, indicating that by this time, the deities of Hongū and Hayatama were also enshrined there. Thus, by the end of the 12th century, the three mountains had unified by worshipping each other's deities . == Kumano Gongen == Each of the Three Mountains is considered to represent a different pure land: Hongū represents the [[Sukhavati|Western Paradise]], Shingu represents the eastern pure land of Lapis Lazuli{{Efn|the eastern pure land of Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa "Pure Lapis Lazuli" ruled by {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}}}}, and Nachi represents the Southern Potalaka{{efn|Ratnasambhava, the Buddha of the Southern Pure Land|12=draft}}. From the [[Heian period]] onward, Kumano as a whole came to be regarded as a land of the Pure Land. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en|12=draft}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|1=Bhaisajyaguru|lt=Yakushi Nyorai (Me)dicine Buddha|en|12=draft}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en:draft|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|12=fr|12=draft}} {{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}} The {{ill|Nachi Falls|en}} is said to be the thirteenth member.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|url=https://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/en/kumano-sanzan/nachi.html|access-date=2024-03-24|website=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|language=en|12=draft}} At {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en}} and {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en|12=draft}}, twelve deities are enshrined as follows. {| class="wikitable" |+'''Kumano Twelve Shrines GongenMiyaie [1992: 60] according to the table''' ! The current deity of [[Kumano Taisha|Kumano-taisha]] is "{{Nihongo|2=熊野大神櫛御気野命|3=Kumano Oyagami Kushimitama no Mikoto}}," but there is a theory that the original deity was Kumanokusubi. There is a theory that the deity of {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en}}, {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|qq=draft}}, is [[Izanami|Izamiami]], but this is also believed to be a reference to Kumanokusubi.{{Cite book|title="Nihon no kami yomi kakkai jiten"|publisher=Kashiwa Shobo|others=Kawaguchi Kenji (ed.)|year=1999|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3|language=ja}} The religious significance of the Kumano region goes back to prehistoric times and therefore predates all modern religions in Japan. The area is still considered a place of physical healing. Each shrine initially had its own separate form of nature worship. In the 10th century, under the influence of Buddhism, the three came to be worshiped together as the three deities of Kumano. Because at the time Japanese ''kami'' were believed to be emanations of {{ill|Buddha|lt=buddhas|en|qq=draft}} (''{{ill|honji suijaku|en}}'' theory), the three came to be associated with Buddhas. Kuniyasutamahime became associated with ''Sahasrabhūja'' {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|qq=draft}} (''Senju Kannon'', "{{ill|Avalokiteśvara#Thousand-armed Avalokiteśvara|lt=Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara|en}}"), {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}} (''Yakushi Nyōrai'') and {{ill|Amitābha|en|qq=draft}} (''Amida Nyōrai'').{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sZmMAQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|last1=Breen|first1=John|last2=Teeuwen|first2=Mark|publisher=Taylor & Francis|year=2013|isbn=978-1-136-82704-4|page=194|authorlink1=John Breen (scholar)|authorlink2=Mark Teeuwen}} Kumano Gongen refers to the deities of the Three Kumano Mountains, especially focusing on the main deities: Ketsumiko ({{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊|qq=draft}}), Hayatama ({{ill|Izanagi|lt=Izanagi|ja|イザナギ|qq=draft}}), and Musubi (also written as Fusubi or Musubi, or "Yui" for {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}}), collectively known as the Kumano Sanjo Gongen. In addition to these, other deities are also included, referred to as the Kumano Jūniso Gongen. The site became a unique example of {{ill|shinbutsu-shūgō|en}}, the fusion between Buddhism and Japanese {{ill|ethnic religion|lt=indigenous religion|en|qq=draft}}. The Three Kumano Mountains consist of Kumano Hongū Taisha, Kumano Hayatama Taisha, and Kumano Nachi Taisha.{{Cite web|date=2009-03-03|title=Sacred Site, "Kumano Sanzan"|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=web.archive.org}} Initially, they developed separately; Hongū was established during the reign of [[Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suinin]], Hayatama during [[Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō's]] reign (according to the Fusang Jijin), and Nachi during [[Emperor Kōshō|Emperor Kōshō's]] reign, with the foundation involving a practice called naked pilgrimage (also "naked form") , though this is uncertain. In official histories, the names of the deities can be confirmed in documents from 806, with a record from 766 mentioning that four households were dedicated to the Hayatama and Kumano Musubi deities, indicating that these two deities were worshipped together in what is today Shingu, known as Kumano Shinson.[[Image:Waterfall Nachi02.jpg|thumb|200 px|{{ill|Nachi Falls|en}}]] By the mid-9th century, the deity was simply called Kumano Imasu Kami, and the main deity of Hongū, previously unclear, began to be called Ketsumiko or Shōshō Bosatsu, along with New Musubi and Hayatama, establishing the tradition that Ketsumiko was an ancient Kumano deity ("Kumano Gongen Suijaku Engi", included in "Chōkan Kanmon" ). The Kumano Sanzan site attracted many worshipers and became a popular pilgrimage destination. In the 11th century, pilgrims were mostly members of the {{ill|emperor of Japan|lt=imperial family|en|qq=draft}} or aristocrats, but four centuries later they were mostly commoners. The visit was referred to as the {{nihongo|"Kumano ant pilgrimage"|蟻の熊野参り||Ari no Kumano mairi}}, because they could be seen winding through the valleys like so many ants. Moreover, the "Chūyūki" entry for October 26, 1109, not only lists these three deities but also mentions Goshodenji, Ichiman Kenzoku, Jūman Kongō Dōji, Kanjō Jūgoso, Hikō Yasha, and Meiji Kongō Dōji, and the pilgrimage records of Toba-in and Taikenmon'in (included in "Chōshūki") from February 1, Longsheng 3 year, list the twelve Gongen and their original Buddhas, showing that by this time, the Kumano Sanjo Gongen and Jūniso Gongen were established . Nachi, differing in nature from Hongū and Hayatama and known as a sacred place for waterfall asceticism, initially had {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}} as the main deity, but by the early Kamakura period, the "Kumano Gongen Kongō Zōjō Hōden Constructing Merits Diary" included tales related to the worship of the Twelve Gongen, indicating that by this time, the deities of Hongū and Hayatama were also enshrined there. Thus, by the end of the 12th century, the three mountains had unified by worshipping each other's deities . == Kumano Gongen == Each of the Three Mountains is considered to represent a different pure land: Hongū represents the [[Sukhavati|Western Paradise]], Shingu represents the eastern pure land of Lapis Lazuli{{Efn|the eastern pure land of Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa "Pure Lapis Lazuli" ruled by {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}}}}, and Nachi represents the Southern Potalaka{{efn|Ratnasambhava, the Buddha of the Southern Pure Land|qq=draft}}. From the [[Heian period]] onward, Kumano as a whole came to be regarded as a land of the Pure Land. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en|qq=draft}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|1=Bhaisajyaguru|lt=Yakushi Nyorai (Me)dicine Buddha|en|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en:draft|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|12=fr|qq=draft}} {{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}} The {{ill|Nachi Falls|en}} is said to be the thirteenth member.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|url=https://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/en/kumano-sanzan/nachi.html|access-date=2024-03-24|website=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|language=en|qq=draft}} At {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en}} and {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en|qq=draft}}, twelve deities are enshrined as follows. {| class="wikitable" |+'''Kumano Twelve Shrines GongenMiyaie [1992: 60] according to the table''' ! ||{{ill|Manjushri|ja|文殊菩薩|en|12=fr|qq=draft}}・{{ill|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|lt=Samantabhadra|ja|普賢菩薩|en|12=fr|qq=draft}}||Secular Form |- |Tenth Pavilion||Meiji Kongō||{{ill|Haniyasu-hiko and Haniyasu-hime|lt=Haniyasu-hime-no-Mikoto|ja|ハニヤス|en|qq=draft}}||{{ill|Vaishravana|ja|毘沙門天|en|12=fr|qq=draft}}||Secular Form |- |Eleventh Pavilion||Flying Yasha||{{ill|Mizuhanome|lt=Mizuhanome-no-Mikoto|ja|ミヅハノメ|en|qq=draft}}||{{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王|1=Acala|lt=Fudō Myōō|2=ja|3=不動明王|en|12=fr|qq=draft}}||Yasha Form |- |Twelfth Pavilion||Kanjō Jūgosho||{{ill|Wakumusubi|lt=Wakumusubi-no-Mikoto|ja|ワクムスビ|en|qq=draft}}||{{ill|Gautama Buddha|ja|釈迦如来|12=fr|qq=draft}}||Secular Form |} At Kumano Nachi Taisha, "Taki-miya" (deity {{ill|Ōkuninushi|lt=Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto|ja|大己貴命|qq=draft}} (Takinawa Gongen), original Buddha Thousand-Armed Kannon) is considered the first pavilion, and the order descends one pavilion at a time, enshrining the eight deities of the Middle Four Shrines and the Lower Four Shrines in the sixth pavilion (Hassha-den), thus known as the "Thirteen Shrines Gongen". ==See also== *{{ill|Kasuga-no-Kami|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-no-Kami|en:draft|Kasuga-no-Kami|ja|春日神|qq=draft}} *{{ill|Kumano Shrine (Yamagata)|en}} *''{{ill|The Tale of the Heike|en|qq=draft}}'' *''{{ill|Acts of Worship|en}}'' == Notes == {{Reflist|2|qq=draft}} == References == * {{cite book|title=Japanese Buddhism — A Cultural History|last=Tamura|first=Yoshiro|publisher=Kosei Publishing Company|year=2000|isbn=4-333-01684-3|edition=First|location=Tokyo|pages=232 pages|language=}} * {{cite book|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|last=[[John Breen (scholar)|Breen, John]]|first=[[Mark Teeuwen|Mark Teeuwen]] (editors)|date=July 2000|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-2363-4|location=Honolulu|language=|oclc=43487317}} {{Commons Category|Gongen }} * == Notes == {{Reflist}} == References == * D. {{draft}} {{Infobox deity|image=Three-storied_Pagoda_of_Seiganto-ji_and_Nachi_Falls_201808.jpg|caption=Three-storied [[Pagoda|Pagoda]] of {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Nachi Falls|en|qq=draft}}|name=Kumano Gongen|cult_centre={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|cult_center={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|qq=draft}}}} {{complex}} {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano (deity)|lt=Kumano|ja|熊野権現|en|Draft:Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|qq=draft}}|熊野権現}}, also known as {{nihongo|Three Mountains of Kumano|熊野三山}}Encyclopedia of Shinto, [http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1076 Kumano Shinkō], accessed on October 6, 2008[http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm Kumano Sanzan] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609225919/http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm|date=2008-06-09}}, World Heritage Registration Association, accessed on October 13, 2008, is a Japanese deity associated with [[Kumano shrine|Kumano Shrines]].{{Cite web|date=2022-07-04|title=Discover the unique spiritual culture of Kumano with exclusive insight from a chief priest at Kumano Hongu Taisha|url=https://www.the-kansai-guide.com/en/article/item/20036/|access-date=2024-03-11|website=The KANSAI Guide - The Origin of Japan, KANSAI|language=en}} The kami enshrined in the three Kumano Sanzan Grand Shrines and worshipped in [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrines]] are the three Kumano mountains: Hongū, Shingū, and Nachi. There are more than 3,000 Kumano shrines in [[Japan|Japan]], and each has received its [[kami|kami]] from another Kumano shrine through a process of propagation called {{ill|''{{ill|bunrei|en}}''|分霊|1=Bunrei}} or {{ill|''{{ill|kanjō|en}}''|勧請|lt=Enshrinement|1=Kanjō|2=ja|3=分霊|4=es|5=Bunrei|6=id|7=Kanjō|8=zh|9=分靈|10=fr|11=Kanjō|lt=Kanjō}}. They are connected to each other by the pilgrimage route known as {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|熊野古道|qq=draft}}. The great Kumano Sanzan complex also includes two Buddhist temples, {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Fudarakusan-ji|en|qq=draft}}.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Sanzan|url=http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822161901/http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|archive-date=2019-08-22|access-date=2014-10-15}} {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|qq=draft}}, the fifth and youngest child of [[Amaterasu]] is sometimes linked to Kumano Gongen The deity's name, Kusubi (Kusuhi), is thought to mean "strange spirit" (mysterious divine spirit) or "strange fire. From the [[Heian period]] onward, Kumano as a whole came to be regarded as a land of the Pure Land. {{Infobox deity|image=Three-storied_Pagoda_of_Seiganto-ji_and_Nachi_Falls_201808.jpg|caption=Three-storied [[Pagoda|Pagoda]] of {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Nachi Falls|en|qq=draft}}|name=Kumano Gongen|cult_centre={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|cult_center={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|qq=draft}}}} {{complex}} {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano (deity)|lt=Kumano|ja|熊野権現|en|Draft:Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|qq=draft}}|熊野権現}}, also known as {{nihongo|Three Mountains of Kumano|熊野三山}}Encyclopedia of Shinto, [http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1076 Kumano Shinkō], accessed on October 6, 2008[http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm Kumano Sanzan] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609225919/http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm|date=2008-06-09}}, World Heritage Registration Association, accessed on October 13, 2008, is a Japanese deity associated with [[Kumano shrine|Kumano Shrines]].{{Cite web|date=2022-07-04|title=Discover the unique spiritual culture of Kumano with exclusive insight from a chief priest at Kumano Hongu Taisha|url=https://www.the-kansai-guide.com/en/article/item/20036/|access-date=2024-03-11|website=The KANSAI Guide - The Origin of Japan, KANSAI|language=en}} The kami enshrined in the three Kumano Sanzan Grand Shrines and worshipped in [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrines]] are the three Kumano mountains: Hongū, Shingū, and Nachi. There are more than 3,000 Kumano shrines in [[Japan|Japan]], and each has received its [[kami|kami]] from another Kumano shrine through a process of propagation called {{ill|''{{ill|bunrei|en}}''|分霊|1=Bunrei}} or {{ill|''{{ill|kanjō|en}}''|勧請|lt=Enshrinement|1=Kanjō|2=ja|3=分霊|4=es|5=Bunrei|6=id|7=Kanjō|8=zh|9=分靈|10=fr|11=Kanjō|lt=Kanjō}}. The point of origin of the Kumano cult is the Kumano Sanzan shrine complex in {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en}}, which comprises {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en|qq=draft}}|熊野速玉大社}} ({{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en}}), {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en}}) and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Nachikatsuura|en}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|qq=draft}}).{{Cite web|title=Sacred site "Kumano Sanzan"|url=http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|archive-date=2009-03-03|access-date=2008-06-12}} == Origins == [[Image:Kumano Jinja 12.jpg|275 px|thumb|A [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrine]]]]The three Kumano Sanzan shrines are the ''Sōhonsha'' ("head shrines") of all Kumano shrines and lie between 20 and 40 km from each other. They are connected to each other by the pilgrimage route known as {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|熊野古道|qq=draft}}. The great Kumano Sanzan complex also includes two Buddhist temples, {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Fudarakusan-ji|en|qq=draft}}.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Sanzan|url=http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822161901/http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|archive-date=2019-08-22|access-date=2014-10-15}} {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|qq=draft}}, the fifth and youngest child of [[Amaterasu]] is sometimes linked to Kumano Gongen The deity's name, Kusubi (Kusuhi), is thought to mean "strange spirit" (mysterious divine spirit) or "strange fire. The current deity of [[Kumano Taisha|Kumano-taisha]] is "{{Nihongo|2=熊野大神櫛御気野命|3=Kumano Oyagami Kushimitama no Mikoto}}," but there is a theory that the original deity was Kumanokusubi. There is a theory that the deity of {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en}}, {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|qq=draft}}, is [[Izanami|Izamiami]], but this is also believed to be a reference to Kumanokusubi.{{Cite book|title="Nihon no kami yomi kakkai jiten"|publisher=Kashiwa Shobo|others=Kawaguchi Kenji (ed.)|year=1999|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3|language=ja}} The religious significance of the Kumano region goes back to prehistoric times and therefore predates all modern religions in Japan. The area is still considered a place of physical healing. Each shrine initially had its own separate form of nature worship. In the 10th century, under the influence of Buddhism, the three came to be worshiped together as the three deities of Kumano. Because at the time Japanese ''kami'' were believed to be emanations of {{ill|Buddha|lt=buddhas|en|qq=draft}} (''{{ill|honji suijaku|en}}'' theory), the three came to be associated with Buddhas. Kuniyasutamahime became associated with ''Sahasrabhūja'' {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|qq=draft}} (''Senju Kannon'', "{{ill|Avalokiteśvara#Thousand-armed Avalokiteśvara|lt=Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara|en}}"), {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}} (''Yakushi Nyōrai'') and {{ill|Amitābha|en|qq=draft}} (''Amida Nyōrai'').{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sZmMAQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|last1=Breen|first1=John|last2=Teeuwen|first2=Mark|publisher=Taylor & Francis|year=2013|isbn=978-1-136-82704-4|page=194|authorlink1=John Breen (scholar)|authorlink2=Mark Teeuwen}} Kumano Gongen refers to the deities of the Three Kumano Mountains, especially focusing on the main deities: Ketsumiko ({{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊|qq=draft}}), Hayatama ({{ill|Izanagi|lt=Izanagi|ja|イザナギ|qq=draft}}), and Musubi (also written as Fusubi or Musubi, or "Yui" for {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}}), collectively known as the Kumano Sanjo Gongen. In addition to these, other deities are also included, referred to as the Kumano Jūniso Gongen. The site became a unique example of {{ill|shinbutsu-shūgō|en}}, the fusion between Buddhism and Japanese {{ill|ethnic religion|lt=indigenous religion|en|qq=draft}}. The Three Kumano Mountains consist of Kumano Hongū Taisha, Kumano Hayatama Taisha, and Kumano Nachi Taisha.{{Cite web|date=2009-03-03|title=Sacred Site, "Kumano Sanzan"|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=web.archive.org}} Initially, they developed separately; Hongū was established during the reign of [[Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suinin]], Hayatama during [[Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō's]] reign (according to the Fusang Jijin), and Nachi during [[Emperor Kōshō|Emperor Kōshō's]] reign, with the foundation involving a practice called naked pilgrimage (also "naked form") , though this is uncertain. In official histories, the names of the deities can be confirmed in documents from 806, with a record from 766 mentioning that four households were dedicated to the Hayatama and Kumano Musubi deities, indicating that these two deities were worshipped together in what is today Shingu, known as Kumano Shinson.[[Image:Waterfall Nachi02.jpg|thumb|200 px|{{ill|Nachi Falls|en}}]] By the mid-9th century, the deity was simply called Kumano Imasu Kami, and the main deity of Hongū, previously unclear, began to be called Ketsumiko or Shōshō Bosatsu, along with New Musubi and Hayatama, establishing the tradition that Ketsumiko was an ancient Kumano deity ("Kumano Gongen Suijaku Engi", included in "Chōkan Kanmon" ). The Kumano Sanzan site attracted many worshipers and became a popular pilgrimage destination. In the 11th century, pilgrims were mostly members of the {{ill|emperor of Japan|lt=imperial family|en|qq=draft}} or aristocrats, but four centuries later they were mostly commoners. The visit was referred to as the {{nihongo|"Kumano ant pilgrimage"|蟻の熊野参り||Ari no Kumano mairi}}, because they could be seen winding through the valleys like so many ants. Moreover, the "Chūyūki" entry for October 26, 1109, not only lists these three deities but also mentions Goshodenji, Ichiman Kenzoku, Jūman Kongō Dōji, Kanjō Jūgoso, Hikō Yasha, and Meiji Kongō Dōji, and the pilgrimage records of Toba-in and Taikenmon'in (included in "Chōshūki") from February 1, Longsheng 3 year, list the twelve Gongen and their original Buddhas, showing that by this time, the Kumano Sanjo Gongen and Jūniso Gongen were established . Nachi, differing in nature from Hongū and Hayatama and known as a sacred place for waterfall asceticism, initially had {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}} as the main deity, but by the early Kamakura period, the "Kumano Gongen Kongō Zōjō Hōden Constructing Merits Diary" included tales related to the worship of the Twelve Gongen, indicating that by this time, the deities of Hongū and Hayatama were also enshrined there. Thus, by the end of the 12th century, the three mountains had unified by worshipping each other's deities . == Kumano Gongen == Each of the Three Mountains is considered to represent a different pure land: Hongū represents the [[Sukhavati|Western Paradise]], Shingu represents the eastern pure land of Lapis Lazuli{{Efn|the eastern pure land of Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa "Pure Lapis Lazuli" ruled by {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}}}}, and Nachi represents the Southern Potalaka{{efn|Ratnasambhava, the Buddha of the Southern Pure Land|qq=draft}}. From the [[Heian period]] onward, Kumano as a whole came to be regarded as a land of the Pure Land. {{Infobox deity|image=Three-storied_Pagoda_of_Seiganto-ji_and_Nachi_Falls_201808.jpg|caption=Three-storied [[Pagoda|Pagoda]] of {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Nachi Falls|en|qq=draft}}|name=Kumano Gongen|cult_centre={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|cult_center={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|qq=draft}}}} {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano (deity)|lt=Kumano|ja|熊野権現|en|Draft:Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|qq=draft}}|熊野権現}}, also known as {{nihongo|Three Mountains of Kumano|熊野三山}}Encyclopedia of Shinto, [http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1076 Kumano Shinkō], accessed on October 6, 2008[http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm Kumano Sanzan] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609225919/http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm|date=2008-06-09}}, World Heritage Registration Association, accessed on October 13, 2008, is a Japanese deity associated with [[Kumano shrine|Kumano Shrines]].{{Cite web|date=2022-07-04|title=Discover the unique spiritual culture of Kumano with exclusive insight from a chief priest at Kumano Hongu Taisha|url=https://www.the-kansai-guide.com/en/article/item/20036/|access-date=2024-03-11|website=The KANSAI Guide - The Origin of Japan, KANSAI|language=en}} The kami enshrined in the three Kumano Sanzan Grand Shrines and worshipped in [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrines]] are the three Kumano mountains: Hongū, Shingū, and Nachi. There are more than 3,000 Kumano shrines in [[Japan|Japan]], and each has received its [[kami|kami]] from another Kumano shrine through a process of propagation called {{ill|''{{ill|bunrei|en}}''|分霊|1=Bunrei}} or {{ill|''{{ill|kanjō|en}}''|勧請|lt=Enshrinement|1=Kanjō|2=ja|3=分霊|4=es|5=Bunrei|6=id|7=Kanjō|8=zh|9=分靈|10=fr|11=Kanjō|lt=Kanjō}}. The point of origin of the Kumano cult is the Kumano Sanzan shrine complex in {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en}}, which comprises {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en|qq=draft}}|熊野速玉大社}} ({{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en}}), {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en}}) and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Nachikatsuura|en}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|qq=draft}}).{{Cite web|title=Sacred site "Kumano Sanzan"|url=http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|archive-date=2009-03-03|access-date=2008-06-12}} == Origins == [[Image:Kumano Jinja 12.jpg|275 px|thumb|A [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrine]]]]The three Kumano Sanzan shrines are the ''Sōhonsha'' ("head shrines") of all Kumano shrines and lie between 20 and 40 km from each other. They are connected to each other by the pilgrimage route known as {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|熊野古道|qq=draft}}. The great Kumano Sanzan complex also includes two Buddhist temples, {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Fudarakusan-ji|en|qq=draft}}.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Sanzan|url=http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822161901/http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|archive-date=2019-08-22|access-date=2014-10-15}} {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|qq=draft}}, the fifth and youngest child of [[Amaterasu]] is sometimes linked to Kumano Gongen The deity's name, Kusubi (Kusuhi), is thought to mean "strange spirit" (mysterious divine spirit) or "strange fire. The current deity of [[Kumano Taisha|Kumano-taisha]] is "{{Nihongo|2=熊野大神櫛御気野命|3=Kumano Oyagami Kushimitama no Mikoto}}," but there is a theory that the original deity was Kumanokusubi. There is a theory that the deity of {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en}}, {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|qq=draft}}, is [[Izanami|Izamiami]], but this is also believed to be a reference to Kumanokusubi.{{Cite book|title="Nihon no kami yomi kakkai jiten"|publisher=Kashiwa Shobo|others=Kawaguchi Kenji (ed.)|year=1999|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3|language=ja}} The religious significance of the Kumano region goes back to prehistoric times and therefore predates all modern religions in Japan. The area is still considered a place of physical healing. Each shrine initially had its own separate form of nature worship. In the 10th century, under the influence of Buddhism, the three came to be worshiped together as the three deities of Kumano. Because at the time Japanese ''kami'' were believed to be emanations of {{ill|Buddha|lt=buddhas|en|qq=draft}} (''{{ill|honji suijaku|en}}'' theory), the three came to be associated with Buddhas. Kuniyasutamahime became associated with ''Sahasrabhūja'' {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|qq=draft}} (''Senju Kannon'', "{{ill|Avalokiteśvara#Thousand-armed Avalokiteśvara|lt=Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara|en}}"), {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}} (''Yakushi Nyōrai'') and {{ill|Amitābha|en|qq=draft}} (''Amida Nyōrai'').{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sZmMAQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|last1=Breen|first1=John|last2=Teeuwen|first2=Mark|publisher=Taylor & Francis|year=2013|isbn=978-1-136-82704-4|page=194|authorlink1=John Breen (scholar)|authorlink2=Mark Teeuwen}} Kumano Gongen refers to the deities of the Three Kumano Mountains, especially focusing on the main deities: Ketsumiko ({{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊|qq=draft}}), Hayatama ({{ill|Izanagi|lt=Izanagi|ja|イザナギ|qq=draft}}), and Musubi (also written as Fusubi or Musubi, or "Yui" for {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}}), collectively known as the Kumano Sanjo Gongen. In addition to these, other deities are also included, referred to as the Kumano Jūniso Gongen. The site became a unique example of {{ill|shinbutsu-shūgō|en}}, the fusion between Buddhism and Japanese {{ill|ethnic religion|lt=indigenous religion|en|qq=draft}}. The Three Kumano Mountains consist of Kumano Hongū Taisha, Kumano Hayatama Taisha, and Kumano Nachi Taisha.{{Cite web|date=2009-03-03|title=Sacred Site, "Kumano Sanzan"|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=web.archive.org}} Initially, they developed separately; Hongū was established during the reign of [[Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suinin]], Hayatama during [[Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō's]] reign (according to the Fusang Jijin), and Nachi during [[Emperor Kōshō|Emperor Kōshō's]] reign, with the foundation involving a practice called naked pilgrimage (also "naked form") , though this is uncertain. In official histories, the names of the deities can be confirmed in documents from 806, with a record from 766 mentioning that four households were dedicated to the Hayatama and Kumano Musubi deities, indicating that these two deities were worshipped together in what is today Shingu, known as Kumano Shinson.[[Image:Waterfall Nachi02.jpg|thumb|200 px|{{ill|Nachi Falls|en}}]] By the mid-9th century, the deity was simply called Kumano Imasu Kami, and the main deity of Hongū, previously unclear, began to be called Ketsumiko or Shōshō Bosatsu, along with New Musubi and Hayatama, establishing the tradition that Ketsumiko was an ancient Kumano deity ("Kumano Gongen Suijaku Engi", included in "Chōkan Kanmon" ). The Kumano Sanzan site attracted many worshipers and became a popular pilgrimage destination. In the 11th century, pilgrims were mostly members of the {{ill|emperor of Japan|lt=imperial family|en|qq=draft}} or aristocrats, but four centuries later they were mostly commoners. The visit was referred to as the {{nihongo|"Kumano ant pilgrimage"|蟻の熊野参り||Ari no Kumano mairi}}, because they could be seen winding through the valleys like so many ants. Moreover, the "Chūyūki" entry for October 26, 1109, not only lists these three deities but also mentions Goshodenji, Ichiman Kenzoku, Jūman Kongō Dōji, Kanjō Jūgoso, Hikō Yasha, and Meiji Kongō Dōji, and the pilgrimage records of Toba-in and Taikenmon'in (included in "Chōshūki") from February 1, Longsheng 3 year, list the twelve Gongen and their original Buddhas, showing that by this time, the Kumano Sanjo Gongen and Jūniso Gongen were established . Nachi, differing in nature from Hongū and Hayatama and known as a sacred place for waterfall asceticism, initially had {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}} as the main deity, but by the early Kamakura period, the "Kumano Gongen Kongō Zōjō Hōden Constructing Merits Diary" included tales related to the worship of the Twelve Gongen, indicating that by this time, the deities of Hongū and Hayatama were also enshrined there. Thus, by the end of the 12th century, the three mountains had unified by worshipping each other's deities . == Kumano Gongen == Each of the Three Mountains is considered to represent a different pure land: Hongū represents the [[Sukhavati|Western Paradise]], Shingu represents the eastern pure land of Lapis Lazuli{{Efn|the eastern pure land of Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa "Pure Lapis Lazuli" ruled by {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}}}}, and Nachi represents the Southern Potalaka{{efn|Ratnasambhava, the Buddha of the Southern Pure Land|qq=draft}}. From the [[Heian period]] onward, Kumano as a whole came to be regarded as a land of the Pure Land. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en|qq=draft}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|1=Bhaisajyaguru|lt=Yakushi Nyorai (Me)dicine Buddha|en|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en:draft|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|12=fr|qq=draft}} {{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}} The {{ill|Nachi Falls|en}} is said to be the thirteenth member.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|url=https://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/en/kumano-sanzan/nachi.html|access-date=2024-03-24|website=Kumano Nachi Taisha｜Wakayama Prefecture World Heritage Center|language=en|qq=draft}} At {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en}} and {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en|qq=draft}}, twelve deities are enshrined as follows. {| class="wikitable" |+'''Kumano Twelve Shrines GongenMiyaie [1992: 60] according to the table''' ! {{Infobox deity|image=Three-storied_Pagoda_of_Seiganto-ji_and_Nachi_Falls_201808.jpg|caption=Three-storied [[Pagoda|Pagoda]] of {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Nachi Falls|en|qq=draft}}|name=Kumano Gongen|cult_centre={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|cult_center={{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|qq=draft}}}} {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano (deity)|lt=Kumano|ja|熊野権現|en|Draft:Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|qq=draft}}|熊野権現}}, also known as {{nihongo|Three Mountains of Kumano|熊野三山}}Encyclopedia of Shinto, [http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1076 Kumano Shinkō], accessed on October 6, 2008[http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm Kumano Sanzan] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609225919/http://www.sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/s_sanzan.htm|date=2008-06-09}}, World Heritage Registration Association, accessed on October 13, 2008, is a Japanese deity associated with [[Kumano shrine|Kumano Shrines]].{{Cite web|date=2022-07-04|title=Discover the unique spiritual culture of Kumano with exclusive insight from a chief priest at Kumano Hongu Taisha|url=https://www.the-kansai-guide.com/en/article/item/20036/|access-date=2024-03-11|website=The KANSAI Guide - The Origin of Japan, KANSAI|language=en}} The kami enshrined in the three Kumano Sanzan Grand Shrines and worshipped in [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrines]] are the three Kumano mountains: Hongū, Shingū, and Nachi. There are more than 3,000 Kumano shrines in [[Japan|Japan]], and each has received its [[kami|kami]] from another Kumano shrine through a process of propagation called {{ill|''{{ill|bunrei|en}}''|分霊|1=Bunrei}} or {{ill|''{{ill|kanjō|en}}''|勧請|lt=Enshrinement|1=Kanjō|2=ja|3=分霊|4=es|5=Bunrei|6=id|7=Kanjō|8=zh|9=分靈|10=fr|11=Kanjō|lt=Kanjō}}. The point of origin of the Kumano cult is the Kumano Sanzan shrine complex in {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en}}, which comprises {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|en|qq=draft}}|熊野速玉大社}} ({{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en}}), {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en}}) and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Nachikatsuura|en}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|qq=draft}}).{{Cite web|title=Sacred site "Kumano Sanzan"|url=http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|archive-date=2009-03-03|access-date=2008-06-12}} == Origins == [[Image:Kumano Jinja 12.jpg|275 px|thumb|A [[Kumano shrine|Kumano shrine]]]]The three Kumano Sanzan shrines are the ''Sōhonsha'' ("head shrines") of all Kumano shrines and lie between 20 and 40 km from each other. They are connected to each other by the pilgrimage route known as {{nihongo|{{ill|Kumano Kodō|en}}|熊野古道|qq=draft}}. The great Kumano Sanzan complex also includes two Buddhist temples, {{ill|Seiganto-ji|en}} and {{ill|Fudarakusan-ji|en|qq=draft}}.{{Cite web|title=Kumano Sanzan|url=http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822161901/http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano_sanzan/|archive-date=2019-08-22|access-date=2014-10-15}} {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|qq=draft}}, the fifth and youngest child of [[Amaterasu]] is sometimes linked to Kumano Gongen The deity's name, Kusubi (Kusuhi), is thought to mean "strange spirit" (mysterious divine spirit) or "strange fire. The current deity of [[Kumano Taisha|Kumano-taisha]] is "{{Nihongo|2=熊野大神櫛御気野命|3=Kumano Oyagami Kushimitama no Mikoto}}," but there is a theory that the original deity was Kumanokusubi. There is a theory that the deity of {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|en}}, {{ill|Kumanokusubi|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kumanokusubi|qq=draft}}, is [[Izanami|Izamiami]], but this is also believed to be a reference to Kumanokusubi.{{Cite book|title="Nihon no kami yomi kakkai jiten"|publisher=Kashiwa Shobo|others=Kawaguchi Kenji (ed.)|year=1999|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3|language=ja}} The religious significance of the Kumano region goes back to prehistoric times and therefore predates all modern religions in Japan. The area is still considered a place of physical healing. Each shrine initially had its own separate form of nature worship. In the 10th century, under the influence of Buddhism, the three came to be worshiped together as the three deities of Kumano. Because at the time Japanese ''kami'' were believed to be emanations of {{ill|Buddha|lt=buddhas|en|qq=draft}} (''{{ill|honji suijaku|en}}'' theory), the three came to be associated with Buddhas. Kuniyasutamahime became associated with ''Sahasrabhūja'' {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|qq=draft}} (''Senju Kannon'', "{{ill|Avalokiteśvara#Thousand-armed Avalokiteśvara|lt=Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara|en}}"), {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}} (''Yakushi Nyōrai'') and {{ill|Amitābha|en|qq=draft}} (''Amida Nyōrai'').{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sZmMAQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|last1=Breen|first1=John|last2=Teeuwen|first2=Mark|publisher=Taylor & Francis|year=2013|isbn=978-1-136-82704-4|page=194|authorlink1=John Breen (scholar)|authorlink2=Mark Teeuwen}} Kumano Gongen refers to the deities of the Three Kumano Mountains, especially focusing on the main deities: Ketsumiko ({{ill|Susanoo|1=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|素戔嗚尊|qq=draft}}), Hayatama ({{ill|Izanagi|lt=Izanagi|ja|イザナギ|qq=draft}}), and Musubi (also written as Fusubi or Musubi, or "Yui" for {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}}), collectively known as the Kumano Sanjo Gongen. In addition to these, other deities are also included, referred to as the Kumano Jūniso Gongen. The site became a unique example of {{ill|shinbutsu-shūgō|en}}, the fusion between Buddhism and Japanese {{ill|ethnic religion|lt=indigenous religion|en|qq=draft}}. The Three Kumano Mountains consist of Kumano Hongū Taisha, Kumano Hayatama Taisha, and Kumano Nachi Taisha.{{Cite web|date=2009-03-03|title=Sacred Site, "Kumano Sanzan"|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303221919/http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/sekaiisan/english/e-kumano_e.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=web.archive.org}} Initially, they developed separately; Hongū was established during the reign of [[Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suinin]], Hayatama during [[Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō's]] reign (according to the Fusang Jijin), and Nachi during [[Emperor Kōshō|Emperor Kōshō's]] reign, with the foundation involving a practice called naked pilgrimage (also "naked form") , though this is uncertain. In official histories, the names of the deities can be confirmed in documents from 806, with a record from 766 mentioning that four households were dedicated to the Hayatama and Kumano Musubi deities, indicating that these two deities were worshipped together in what is today Shingu, known as Kumano Shinson.[[Image:Waterfall Nachi02.jpg|thumb|200 px|{{ill|Nachi Falls|en}}]] By the mid-9th century, the deity was simply called Kumano Imasu Kami, and the main deity of Hongū, previously unclear, began to be called Ketsumiko or Shōshō Bosatsu, along with New Musubi and Hayatama, establishing the tradition that Ketsumiko was an ancient Kumano deity ("Kumano Gongen Suijaku Engi", included in "Chōkan Kanmon" ). The Kumano Sanzan site attracted many worshipers and became a popular pilgrimage destination. In the 11th century, pilgrims were mostly members of the {{ill|emperor of Japan|lt=imperial family|en|qq=draft}} or aristocrats, but four centuries later they were mostly commoners. The visit was referred to as the {{nihongo|"Kumano ant pilgrimage"|蟻の熊野参り||Ari no Kumano mairi}}, because they could be seen winding through the valleys like so many ants. Moreover, the "Chūyūki" entry for October 26, 1109, not only lists these three deities but also mentions Goshodenji, Ichiman Kenzoku, Jūman Kongō Dōji, Kanjō Jūgoso, Hikō Yasha, and Meiji Kongō Dōji, and the pilgrimage records of Toba-in and Taikenmon'in (included in "Chōshūki") from February 1, Longsheng 3 year, list the twelve Gongen and their original Buddhas, showing that by this time, the Kumano Sanjo Gongen and Jūniso Gongen were established . Nachi, differing in nature from Hongū and Hayatama and known as a sacred place for waterfall asceticism, initially had {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}} as the main deity, but by the early Kamakura period, the "Kumano Gongen Kongō Zōjō Hōden Constructing Merits Diary" included tales related to the worship of the Twelve Gongen, indicating that by this time, the deities of Hongū and Hayatama were also enshrined there. Thus, by the end of the 12th century, the three mountains had unified by worshipping each other's deities . == Kumano Gongen == Each of the Three Mountains is considered to represent a different pure land: Hongū represents the [[Sukhavati|Western Paradise]], Shingu represents the eastern pure land of Lapis Lazuli{{Efn|the eastern pure land of Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa "Pure Lapis Lazuli" ruled by {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en}}}}, and Nachi represents the Southern Potalaka{{efn|Ratnasambhava, the Buddha of the Southern Pure Land|qq=draft}}. From the [[Heian period]] onward, Kumano as a whole came to be regarded as a land of the Pure Land. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en|qq=draft}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|1=Bhaisajyaguru|lt=Yakushi Nyorai (Me)dicine Buddha|en|qq=draft}} and
